extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of psychology/psychoanalysis, literary critics, and researchers of humor theory
extracted.subtask_description: Identify, classify, and reduce the technical methods by which jokes produce their effect (e.g., displacement, double meaning, unification, sophistry, automatic habit). Focus is on the psychical processes of joke construction rather than reception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish joke-work from understanding
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not confuse the psychical processes involved in the construction of the joke (the ‘joke-work’) with the psychical processes involved in taking in the joke (the work of understanding). The present enquiry is only concerned with the former.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing or producing jokes, focus on mechanisms that create the joke (how it's produced) rather than the cognitive/emotional response of the hearer. Use reduction methods to expose the construction. (See later chapters for reception.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Displacement
rubrics_metrics.description: Displacement habitually takes place between a remark and a reply which pursues the train of thought in a direction other than that in which it was started by the original remark.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for replies that 'leap' to an unexpected element of the original remark (e.g., the horse-dealer/Pressburg example). In analysis, identify the original semantic track and the direction to which the reply displaces it. Displacement is often combined with double meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Double meaning (ambiguity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of a word or phrase that admits of more than one meaning, which the reply exploits or retroactively claims to have intended.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify lexical ambiguities (e.g., ‘living’ meaning alive vs. ‘that’s not living’) that the joker exploits. Note when double meaning is combined with displacement to produce the punchline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterizing joke / façade of character
rubrics_metrics.description: Joke presents an example intended to illustrate a character’s traits (e.g., mendacious impudence and readiness of repartee) which may form only the outer shell or façade of the joke; the real purpose lies deeper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish surface character-sketches from the underlying technical mechanism producing the joke’s meaning; don’t accept character portrayal as the full explanation without reduction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonsense to reveal another nonsense
rubrics_metrics.description: Presenting something stupid or nonsensical whose sense lies in revealing or demonstrating another piece of stupidity or nonsense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze how an ostensibly absurd remark (e.g., 'buy yourself a cannon') mirrors or exposes stupidity elsewhere (the target’s own foolishness). Reduction should show the secondary piece of nonsense being highlighted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bewilderment and illumination
rubrics_metrics.description: The joke produces an alternation between bewilderment and sudden illumination; bewildering or nonsensical surface that then leads to an illuminating (often obscene or unexpected) meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize when a joke deliberately bewildering on the surface later resolves into an illuminating reinterpretation. Example: the professor’s 'human hands' comment that yields an obscene sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appearance of logic / sophistry
rubrics_metrics.description: A façade of logical reasoning (sophistry) conceals faulty reasoning: treating separate defects in isolation or otherwise misapplying logical operations to hide the overall absurdity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spot arguments that seem logical but improperly isolate elements (e.g., marriage-broker treating defects separately) or combine mutually exclusive claims. Reduction should expose the logical fallacy (e.g., 'put an "and" where only an "either-or" is possible').

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructing invalid connections (false linking)
rubrics_metrics.description: Using double meaning or equivocation to construct a connection that does not exist in reality (e.g., treating two independent processes as if they were exchangeable).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify when the joker equivocates terms or retroactively links independent events (pastry/liqueur example). The humor often lies in the absurdity of the inferred connection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Automatic action / habitual repetition
rubrics_metrics.description: Automatic repetition of a response pattern (habit) in an unsuitable context, producing a comic effect by defeating the speaker’s purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for repeated confirmation or echoing that becomes maladaptive (e.g., assistant echoing praise including the admitted hump). This technique overlaps with comic self-betrayal and can blur joke vs comic anecdote.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unification
rubrics_metrics.description: Setting up a new, unexpected unity between ideas (relations of ideas to one another or to a common third element) so that two things are humorously equated or mirrored.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detect cases where the punchline establishes an unexpected symmetry or mutual definition (e.g., 'Human life falls into two halves...' or repartee that 'turns the tables'). Unification can be achieved by parallel phrasing, shared relation to a third element, or clever mutual reference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple use of the same material / condensation
rubrics_metrics.description: Reusing the same words or material multiple times in different senses (approximate to double meaning or condensation) to create a compact, layered effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note economy of wording where one phrase bears several roles or senses; this produces a concentrated comic effect akin to condensation in other unconscious processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stringing with 'and' / joking enumeration (co-ordination)
rubrics_metrics.description: Using a coordinated list connected by 'and' to imply an unexpected equivalence or relation among items, producing a comic grouping.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine enumerations where the conjunction implies a psychological or categorical link (Heine’s 'students, professors, philistines and donkeys'). The juxtaposition and placement can create irony or reveal attitudes (e.g., placing 'caning' between subjects).

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation by the opposite (yes-but = no)
rubrics_metrics.description: Replacing the only expected answer ('no') by its opposite ('yes') combined with a 'but' so that the surface affirmation functions as a negation (e.g., 'Yes, at your Majesty's command. But they don't come.').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for constructions where an apparent affirmation followed by a qualifying 'but' serves the role of negation or inversion; this reversal is a discrete technical device in many jokes (also used to admire by contrast).

rubrics_metrics.name: Repartee / tu quoque (turning tables)
rubrics_metrics.description: A quick retort that meets an aggression by turning it back on the aggressor, establishing an unexpected unity between attack and counter-attack.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess speed, symmetry, and clever mirroring of the retort (e.g., baker/innkeeper whitlow exchange). Repartee often relies on unification or representation-by-opposite techniques and is valued for its promptness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduction (analytic reconstruction)
rubrics_metrics.description: The method of reducing a joke to its core thought: removing the façade/logic to reveal the underlying faulty reasoning or unconscious motivation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing jokes, perform a reduction—translate the surface wording into the fundamental proposition it masks (examples provided throughout: Schnorrer, cannon, father/daughter screen). Reduction helps reveal which technical device is operative.
